Communication dated May 3, 1972, to the State Clearinghouse from State Forester, South Carolina Forestry Commission.
Comment: The South Carolina Forestry Commission suggests that the proposed legislation provide for consideration of alternative and opposing uses of land proposed for dedication to endangered species habitat. They feel benefits, costs, and adverse effects of such uses be considered before land is set aside exclusively for endangered species.
Certainly, acceptability of other uses of lands set aside for endangered species will be considered, particularly where these lands are already in public ownership. One of the criteria that must be considered in determining the use of a particular tract of land is the uniqueness or scarcity of the resource involved. By definition, endangered species are a unique resource and exclusive use of a tract of land for that purpose is justified. Of course, there may be other resources that are equally rare and, if these uses are incompatible, a decision must be made on their comparative uniqueness. For the most part, land uses such as mineral extraction, timber production, hunting, agriculture, and recreation, when they may not be compatible, are available on other lands and are not unique. Quality endangered species habitat can be very limited and will be confined to the historical range of the species. In summary, we believe that South Carolina's concern over competing uses will be satisfactorily mitigated in most cases. We must accept exclusive use of some tracts for endangered species. In case of a critical shortage of a resource whose extraction or use conflicts with endangered species use, Congress always has the power to change the use through amendment of the Act.
